import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 503

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/503](https://www.erdosproblems.com/503)
-/

namespace Erdos503

open scoped EuclideanGeometry

/--
What is the size of the largest $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ such that every three points from $A$
determine an isosceles triangle? That is, for any three points $x$, $y$, $z$ from $A$, at least two
of the distances $|x - y|$, $|y - z|$, $|x - z|$ are equal.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem erdos_503 (n : ℕ) :
    IsGreatest {(A.ncard) | (A : Set (ℝ^n)) (hA : A.IsIsosceles)} answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
When $n = 2$, the answer is 6 (due to Kelly [ErKe47] - an alternative proof is given by Kovács [Ko24c]).

[ErKe47] Erdős, Paul and Kelly, L. M., Elementary Problems and Solutions: Solutions: E735. Amer. Math. Monthly (1947), 227-229.
[Ko24c] Z. Kovács, A note on Erdős's mysterious remark. arXiv:2412.05190 (2024).
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 51]
theorem erdos_503.variants.R2 :
    IsGreatest {(A.ncard) | (A : Set ℝ²) (hA : A.IsIsosceles)} 6 := by
  sorry

/--
When $n = 3$, the answer is 8 (due to Croft [Cr62]).

[Cr62] Croft, H. T., $9$-point and $7$-point configurations in $3$-space. Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) (1962), 400-424.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 51]
theorem erdos_503.variants.R3 :
    IsGreatest {(A.ncard) | (A : Set ℝ³) (hA : A.IsIsosceles)} 8 := by
  sorry

/--
The best upper bound known in general is due to Blokhius [Bl84] who showed that
$$
|A| \leq \binom{n + 2}{2}
$$

[Bl84] Blokhuis, A., Few-distance sets. (1984), iv+70.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 51]
theorem erdos_503.variants.upper_bound (n : ℕ) :
    ∀ m ∈ {(A.ncard) | (A : Set (ℝ^n)) (hA : A.IsIsosceles)}, m ≤ (n + 2).choose 2 := by
  sorry

/--
Alweiss has observed a lower bound of $\binom{n + 1}{2}$ follows from considering the subset of
$\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$ formed of all vectors $e_i + e_j$ where $e_i$, $e_j$ are distinct coordinate
vectors. This set can be viewed as a subset of some $\mathbb{R}^n$, and is easily checked to have
the required property.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 51]
theorem erdos_503.variants.lower_bound (n : ℕ) :
    (n + 1).choose 2 ≤ sSup {(A.ncard) | (A : Set (ℝ^n)) (hA : A.IsIsosceles)} := by
  sorry

end Erdos503

reformulations.difference: Uses a greatest natural-number cardinality over nonempty, triplewise-isosceles sets, rather than ordinary cardinalities and the source’s all-triples distance condition.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Repeated-point triples automatically satisfy the distance condition. Singletons are admissible, so excluding the empty set cannot affect the maximum. A uniform ncard bound k also excludes infinite admissible sets: an infinite such set would contain an admissible finite subset of size k+1. Consequently, IsGreatest here specifies exactly an attained greatest actual cardinality. Generic equivalences were proved in scratch. The additional dimension-zero case has maximum 1 and is consistent.

reformulations.difference: Expresses the maximum 6 using IsGreatest and Set.ncard, without an explicit finiteness restriction.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The generic greatest-cardinality equivalence proved in scratch applies with ambient space ℝ² and k=6. Its upper-bound component rules out infinite sets through their finite subsets, while its membership component supplies a six-point witness. Thus this is precisely the maximum-size assertion in the source.

reformulations.difference: Expresses the maximum 8 using IsGreatest and Set.ncard, without an explicit finiteness restriction.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The same proved generic equivalence applies with ambient space ℝ³ and k=8: membership supplies an eight-point set, and the uniform upper bound excludes every larger finite or infinite admissible set.

reformulations.difference: Bounds the natural cardinalities in a set comprehension; Set.ncard alone would assign zero to an infinite set.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The bound quantifies over every admissible set, and the isosceles property is inherited by nonempty subsets. Any infinite admissible set would therefore produce an admissible finite subset of size (n+2).choose 2 + 1, contradicting the bound. A generic equivalence with an extended-cardinality bound, including the empty set on the source side, was proved without using any sorry-backed theorem.

reformulations.difference: States the lower bound using sSup on ℕ rather than explicitly asserting existence of a sufficiently large isosceles set.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The set of attainable cardinalities contains 1 and is bounded above by the cited Blokhuis bound. A nonempty bounded subset of ℕ contains its supremum, so L ≤ sSup of these cardinalities is equivalent to existence of an admissible A with L ≤ A.ncard. The generic equivalence was proved in Lean with boundedness as an explicit hypothesis; its applicability here follows from the sourced upper bound.

review.notes: All five declarations were checked. The source still marks the general problem open; the stronger lower bound now mentioned there does not invalidate the file’s weaker bound or its solved tag. Experiments and equivalence proofs are in /workspace/review/scratch.lean, which compiles successfully; the named equivalence proofs have no sorryAx dependency. Tests cover empty and singleton sets, dimensions 0 and 1, and the squared-distance condition for Alweiss’s construction in dimensions 0–7. Although some original publication texts were inaccessible, their relevant statements were independently corroborated by the problem page, Kovács, and Ionin. No declaration’s faithfulness remains unresolved.
